opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to see it is to ask where the computation actually lives. With chain of thought in a transformer, the model does a fixed amount of work per token, a fixed number of layers, and then it has to commit to a discrete token. That token gets written out and fed back in, and the model reads its own output as the next input. All the intermediate reasoning has to pass through that bottleneck of language. Every step, you collapse a very rich, high-dimensional internal state down to one choice out of maybe fifty thousand vocabulary items, and then you rebuild from there.

With a recurrent-depth approach, which is what we've been working on, you keep iterating in the hidden space. You take the latent state, run it through the same block again, and again, and the representation keeps getting refined without ever being forced into a word. You can scale how much compute you spend on a given token just by unrolling more iterations at test time. So the "thinking" happens in continuous space rather than in the sequence dimension.

I'd say they're complementary rather than competing. Chain of thought has some real advantages. It's interpretable to a degree, you can read it, and it leans on everything the model learned from human text about how to lay out an argument step by step. But it's also expensive, because you generate lots of tokens. And there's a real question of whether everything a model might want to "think" is easily expressible in words. Some kinds of reasoning, like spatial things, or keeping several hypotheses in superposition, or something closer to intuition, might be much more natural in a continuous latent state than in a verbalized trace.

The recurrent model doesn't need specialized training data that demonstrates reasoning. You just train it with a variable number of iterations, and it learns to use more depth when that helps. And interestingly, when you look at the latent trajectories, you see some fairly structured behavior. Sometimes the state converges to a fixed point quickly for easy tokens. Sometimes you see orbits or rotations in the latent space for harder things like arithmetic. That suggests the model has found its own way to compute that doesn't look like a written-out chain of thought at all.

So the short version: chain of thought scales reasoning horizontally, across more tokens, through the language bottleneck. Recurrence scales it vertically, through more depth, in the hidden representation. My hunch is the best systems will eventually do both, thinking in latent space where that's efficient and verbalizing where it's useful to externalize or communicate.

r001.rationale: It says each transformer reasoning step commits to a discrete token that is fed back as the next input, creating a language bottleneck instead of carrying the full internal state forward.

r002.rationale: It describes recurrence as repeatedly processing a latent state in hidden space, refining the representation across iterations without forcing it into words.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because on the surface they look like they're doing the same thing. In both cases you're spending more compute at test time to get a better answer. But the mechanism is really different.

With a transformer doing chain of thought, every step of reasoning has to be verbalized. The model produces a token, that token gets fed back in, and that's the only channel through which the computation carries forward. So the "state" of the reasoning is literally the text. That's great for interpretability in some sense, you can read it, but it's also a bottleneck. You're forcing the model to compress whatever it's figured out internally down to a discrete symbol from a vocabulary of, say, a hundred thousand tokens, and then re-expand it on the next step. A lot of what the model knows at the end of a forward pass just gets thrown away.

The recurrent approach, at least the way we've been building it with recurrent depth, is that the model iterates in latent space instead. You take the hidden representation, which is this high-dimensional continuous vector, and you run the same block over it again and again. Nothing gets verbalized between iterations. So the model can hold onto things that don't have a clean linguistic form. It can keep multiple hypotheses in superposition, it can refine a representation gradually, and it's not constrained to only think in the kinds of steps that happen to be expressible as English or as code.

And there's a nice side effect, which is that the recurrence gives you a kind of adaptive compute for free. You can decide per token, or per problem, how many iterations to run. With chain of thought you also get adaptive compute, but it's tied up with generating more text, which costs you context length and costs you the overhead of going through the full embedding and unembedding every time.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. The transformer approach has a huge advantage in that the verbalized trace is a form of memory that scales with length. Our recurrent models iterate in place, so the amount of state is fixed by the hidden dimension. If you need to remember a hundred intermediate results, writing them down is just better. So I actually think the right picture is that these are complementary. Chain of thought is good for the parts of reasoning that are genuinely sequential and need external memory, and latent recurrence is good for the parts that are more like intuition, where you just need to think harder about what's already in front of you before you commit to a token.

The thing I find most interesting is what you see when you look inside the recurrent models. The trajectories in latent space are not random. For some tokens the state just converges quickly and sits there. For others, especially ones involving arithmetic, you see these orbital patterns, the representation kind of rotating through a subspace. It looks like the model has learned to use the recurrence as a mechanism, not just as extra depth. And that's something you would never observe in a chain of thought, because the chain of thought only shows you what the model chose to say, not how it got there.

r001.rationale: The response says each reasoning step produces a token that is fed back in and is the only channel carrying computation forward, so the full hidden representation is not directly passed along.

r002.rationale: It describes recurrent models iterating on a persistent hidden representation in latent space and gradually refining it across iterations.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is where the computation happens. With a long chain of thought, a transformer produces intermediate tokens, and those tokens become the context for subsequent steps. So it can work through a problem by writing things down and then reading what it has written.

A recurrent model can instead keep updating a hidden representation. It takes another computational step without necessarily turning that step into a word. That gives it room to carry information that doesn't have a convenient expression in language, or to maintain several possibilities before committing to an answer.

There is an important caveat: a transformer's computation isn't entirely captured by its chain of thought either. It still has rich hidden representations. The difference is that, in the usual autoregressive setup, extending the computation means generating more tokens. With recurrence, you can extend the computation within the hidden state itself.

So I would think of these as two ways of giving a model more time to think: one uses an explicit textual scratchpad, and the other repeatedly refines an internal state. And you can combine the two.

r001.rationale: The response says a transformer generates intermediate tokens that become context for subsequent steps, and contrasts this with extending computation inside the hidden state. This communicates token-mediated information flow between reasoning steps.

r002.rationale: The response says a recurrent model can keep updating a hidden representation across computational steps, including carrying information without expressing it as words.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful distinction is where the computation happens. When a transformer produces a long chain of thought, it writes intermediate steps into tokens. Each new token becomes part of the context, so the model can attend back to those steps and build on them. In that sense, the text acts as a kind of working memory.

A recurrent model can instead keep updating a hidden representation. It can spend additional computation refining that representation without translating every intermediate step into language. That gives it more freedom in how it represents the problem, but it also makes the process harder for us to inspect.

Of course, a transformer's hidden representations are doing a lot of work too, and the written chain of thought isn't necessarily a faithful account of that work. So I wouldn't draw the distinction as one model reasoning and the other not reasoning. It's more about whether you carry intermediate computation forward through explicit tokens or through a latent state.

r001.rationale: The response says a transformer carries intermediate steps forward as tokens in the context, which later steps can attend to, rather than carrying them forward only through a latent state.

r002.rationale: The response says a recurrent model can keep updating and refining a hidden representation across additional computation.
